title: A week of your rule
hookLine: look back at a week of living your rule
tomorrow: Shabbat comes with two commands, said in one breath. which two?

lines: A LINE TURNS INTO A BOX YOU TICK.
cards: A playlist you loved in spring turns into wallpaper by fall. Same songs, and you've stopped hearing them. Rules of life do that too.
A line that felt alive on day one can turn into a box you tick. A sage in the Mishnah, Rabbi Eliezer, saw it happening to prayer and gave a warning that sounds almost like a contradiction.
So do you change a rule that's gone flat, or keep it exactly as it is? The tradition argues both sides.

teach.b: The argument turns on one word. Remember keva, from ten minutes of learning? Shammai, in Pirkei Avot: make your study keva, fixed.
But in Berakhot, Rabbi Eliezer uses the same word as a warning: whoever makes his prayer keva, his prayer is not tachanunim, real pleading. Same word, opposite verdict.

teach.h: HOLD THE LINE, OR WATCH FOR ROT.
teach.b: View one says hold the line. A fixed time and a fixed text carry you through the dull weeks, and a rule you rewrite whenever it feels flat isn't a rule anymore.
Its best case: the days you least feel it are the days the rule exists for. View two says watch for rot. The Talmud asks what Rabbi Eliezer meant by fixed, and gives more than one answer.
One sage: prayer that feels like a burden. Another: prayer you can't add anything new to. Its best case: a rule that's become pure duty has stopped doing the thing it was for.
Put them side by side and you get this week's line. Throwing the rule away loses what view one protects. Letting it go stiff loses what view two protects.

teach.h: CHANGE THE HOUR, SHRINK THE SIZE.
teach.b: So adjust: change the hour, shrink the size, add one new thing.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the same Hebrew word for fixed is a compliment in one Mishnah and a warning in another.

how: Jewish prayer keeps a fixed text and fixed times, and the tradition also encourages adding personal words inside the fixed prayers; teachers of Musar and spiritual direction often suggest reviewing a personal rule weekly and adjusting it rather than dropping it.

games.q: what does “a week of your rule” mean?
o: a week off from all your daily practices
looking back at seven days and tuning your rule
starting a brand-new rule at the end of each week

games.q: one word, two verdicts — tap the pairs.
p: prayer that feels like a burden
prayer you can't add anything new to

s: the Mishnah only ever praises fixed prayer
Rabbi Eliezer warns that a prayer made keva, fixed, is not real pleading.
one Talmud sage says dead prayer is prayer you can't add anything new to
so the cure is something new inside the old frame.
adjusting a rule means you've given up on it
adjust, don't abandon: rewrite the line, keep the rule.

games.q: your study partner wants to rewrite your shared reading plan every week to keep it fresh. you like it fixed. what's her side's best case?
o: a rule that never changes can turn into a burden; something new keeps it alive.
fixed plans are for beginners; serious learners improvise every day.
the Mishnah says a fixed study time is forbidden.
games.why: that's the Berakhot side: prayer gone stiff, a burden, nothing new. your side has its best case too: the dull weeks are what the rule is for.

practice: Write your three-line rule from memory on a scrap of paper. Put a small mark beside the line that didn't happen this week.
Don't cross it out: rewrite it underneath, sooner, smaller or simpler, so it fits the week you actually have.

wordCard.voice: A week of your rule: looking back honestly at seven days of living it, and tuning the line that isn't working instead of dropping the rule.

orig.note: Hebrew: something new; a fresh thought added to an old text or practice.

carryVoice: Your line: adjust, don't abandon. Same rule, one line rewritten for the life you've actually got.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 1:15 (Shammai: make your Torah study fixed)
Mishnah Berakhot 4:4 (Rabbi Eliezer: one who makes his prayer fixed, his prayer is not supplication)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 29b (what is 'fixed': prayer like a burden; not said as supplication; one who cannot add something new to it)
